opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the overall mood among people actually building these models is quite optimistic, and it's a grounded kind of optimism, not hype. When you're inside a lab, you see the curves every day. You see what the next model can do that the last one couldn't, and the gap is still large. So people aren't asking whether progress will continue. They're asking which bottleneck to push on next.

At Anthropic, there's a strong belief that scaling, together with better training methods, especially reinforcement learning on long and realistic tasks, will keep producing much more capable systems. Coding is a good example. A couple of years ago, models could write a function. Now they can work through a real codebase for a long stretch, use tools, recover from mistakes. Many people there think this will extend to most kinds of knowledge work fairly soon. That belief also explains why safety is taken so seriously. You only invest that heavily in alignment and interpretability if you really think the systems will become very powerful.

Google DeepMind and the Gemini team share that conviction, though the emphasis is a bit different. Google has huge compute, its own chips, and a long research tradition, so there's more of a feeling that you can push on many fronts at once: pretraining, multimodality, reasoning, science applications. People there also tend to think in terms of fundamental research breakthroughs, not just engineering scale.

What both places have in common, I'd say, is this: the "we're hitting a wall" narrative you sometimes hear from outside doesn't match what researchers see. Some things do get harder. Data for pretraining is more limited, evaluations saturate quickly, and the RL environments have to be built very carefully. But each time one approach starts to flatten, another opens up. Pretraining scaling, then post-training, then test-time compute and reasoning, then agents working over long horizons. It's a stack of S-curves.

My personal view is that the biggest open question isn't raw intelligence. It's whether models can reliably do long, open-ended work in the real world, the kind where nobody hands you a clean reward signal. That's where I think the next few years of real progress will be decided.

r001.rationale: The response says researchers at Anthropic and Google Gemini are optimistic and reject the idea that progress is hitting a wall, but it does not say they focus more on AI replacing them.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, from what I see, the people actually building these models at both places are more optimistic than the outside discourse would suggest. There's a lot of noise right now about scaling hitting a wall or pretraining running out of data, but inside the labs the feeling is closer to "we have more ideas than we have compute and people to try them."

I think the reason is that the frontier has shifted. In the first half of the field, progress came mostly from scale on pretraining, and you could draw a straight line on a plot. That line did flatten. But what replaced it is a different axis: reinforcement learning on top of strong priors, long-horizon agents, and the ability to put models in environments where they can actually act and get feedback. Everyone at Anthropic and Gemini sees that this second axis is still very steep. Every few months the models go from "can do a ten-minute task" to "can do an hour-long task," and that kind of improvement is not slowing down.

Where the two cultures differ, in my impression, is less about whether progress continues and more about what they're betting on. Anthropic is very focused on coding and agents as the wedge, and on making models reliable enough that people will hand them real work. Google has this enormous advantage in infrastructure, in TPUs, in data from products, and in multimodal, so they tend to think about progress in a broader, more product-shaped way. But if you asked a researcher at either place "will the model two years from now be dramatically better at doing real tasks," I don't think you'd find many who say no.

The thing I'd add, and this is where I'm a bit contrarian, is that the bottleneck is increasingly not the models. It's evaluation and environments. We're good at making models that climb a benchmark. We're less good at asking whether the benchmark measures something that matters, and at building environments that capture real-world messiness. So when people inside the labs talk about outlook, the optimists point at the capability curve, and the people who are a little more careful point at the question of whether we know what we're measuring. I think both are right, and the second problem is the one that will decide how fast the progress actually shows up in the world.

r001.rationale: The candidate says researchers are optimistic about continued progress and discusses scaling concerns, but it does not say they focus more on AI replacing them than on progress hitting a wall.

astra-6.text:
My sense is that both groups are optimistic about continued progress, though I wouldn’t assume everyone at either organization has the same outlook. And I can’t speak for their internal views.

I’d distinguish two questions: will the models keep getting better, and how quickly will that translate into useful capabilities? You can be very optimistic about the first while still being uncertain about the second. A model can improve on benchmarks and still struggle to complete a long task reliably.

So I’d frame the outlook less as ‘Anthropic versus Gemini’ and more as where people expect the next gains to come from—training, reasoning at inference time, or building systems that let models interact with tools and learn from feedback. Those paths can reinforce each other. The harder question is how consistently that progress carries over to real work.

r001.rationale: The response says both groups are optimistic about continued progress and discusses uncertainty about its pace and usefulness. It does not say people in Shunyu Yao’s reach worry more about AI replacing them than progress hitting a wall.

sol-6.1.text:
I can’t speak for the teams at Anthropic or Google Gemini, and I wouldn’t assume that everyone within either organization shares the same outlook. But I’d separate two questions: will models continue to improve, and will those improvements translate into useful capabilities in the real world?

You can be optimistic about the first while still seeing substantial challenges in the second. A model might perform better on a benchmark yet struggle to complete a long task reliably. For agents, progress also depends on how models use tools, interact with their environment, and recover from mistakes.

So the distinction I’d want to understand is less which team is more optimistic and more what each team thinks is the bottleneck—and what evidence would change its view.
